case_name: Shariful Islam v State of Uttar Pradesh
respondent:
State of Uttar Pradesh
Supreme Court of India

26 October 1972
Cr.A. No. 83 of 1969.
The Judgment was delivered by: CHANDRACHUD, J.
1.  The appellant was convicted by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Rampur u/s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for four years. The charge against the appellant is that he had committed breach of trust in regard to a sum of Rs. 499.66 P. The High Court of Allahabad confirmed the judgment of the trial court and being aggrieved thereby the appellant has filed this appeal by special leave.
2.  The appellant, Shariful Islam, was working as a Collection Amin in Tehsil Shahabad from March 1961 to July 1961. One of his duties was to receive the amounts payable to the Government. On March 26, 1961, he is alleged to have received a sum of Rs. 200/- from one Raghubir Singh and a sum of Rs. 300.41 P. from one Sri Ram Pandey through his brother, Paras Ram Pandey. facts: The appellant was convicted by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Rampur u/s. 409 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for four years.
The charge against the appellant is that he had committed breach of trust in regard to a sum of Rs. 499.66 P.
The defence of the appellant was that the two persons had only paid 0.25 P. and 0.50 P. respectively and that he was falsely implicated in the charges as the Tehsildar was hostile to him.

Raghubir Singh has stated in his evidence that he owed a sum of Rs. 2,000/- to the Government towards a Taqavi loan and that he had paid Rs. 200/- to the appellant on March 26, 1961, in part payment of that amount.
A witness called Roshan Singh says that Raghubir Singh had paid the sum of Rs. 200/- to the appellant in his presence.
Similarly the evidence of Paras Ram Pandey shows that he had paid to the appellant, a sum of Rs. 300.41 P., on behalf of his brother, Sri Ram Pandey.
The appellant says in his statement u/s. 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that the Tehsildar was inimical to him but of that there is no evidence whatsoever.
A receipt which was given by the appellant to Raghubir Singh is on the record of the case at Ex. Ka-3.

Habibul Rahman, who was an Assistant Wasil Baqi Navis, has stated in his evidence that the receipt was in the handwriting of the appellant and that the words, 'rupees two hundred' in Hindi were also in the handwriting of the appellant.

The learned Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Rampur who committed the appellant to the Court of Session has observed in the committal order that the particular receipt was tampered with by the appellant during the pendency of the committal proceedings.

Ram Chander Gangwar, who was a Naib-Tehsildar at the relevant time shows that he has checked the receipt given by the appellant to Paras Ram Pandey and that he had prepared the coupon Ex. Ka-5 on the basis of that receipt.

It was urged on behalf of the appellant that an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution because of its failure to produce the demand notice served on Raghubir Singh and Sri Ram Pandey and the recovery list maintained in the Tehsil.
In view of the direct evidence of Raghubir Singh, Roshan Singh and Paras Ram Pandey we do not think that it was necessary for the prosecution to produce these documents.

Learned counsel relied on a decision of the High Court of Allahabad in Surendra Singh v. The State (1953 Indlaw ALL 202 in support of his contention that the order of conviction is erroneous, but the facts there were materially different.

In the instant case, the two particular amounts were paid into the hands of the appellant not only as being due to the Government but the evidence shows that they were in fact due to the Government and the appellant would be guilty of breach of trust, if he misappropriated that amount.

court_reasoning: The High Court was justified in confirming the conviction and sentence of the appellant.

It was common ground that a receipt book was issued by the Shahabad Tehsil to the appellant and that he issued two receipts, Nos. 29 and 50, from out of that book to Raghubir Singh and Sri Ram Pandey.
The evidence of these witnesses is that the admission by them that they owed a particular sum of money to the Government was against their self-interest.
These witnesses have hardly been cross-examined and not even a suggestion has been made to them that they had any reason for implicating the appellant falsely.

Habibul Rahman, who was an Assistant Wasil Baqi Navis, has stated in his evidence that the receipt was in the handwriting of the appellant and that the words, 'rupees two hundred' in Hindi were also in the handwriting of the appellant.

Ram Chander Gangwar, who was a Naib-Tehsildar at the relevant time shows that he has checked the receipt given by the appellant to Paras Ram Pandey and that he had prepared the coupon Ex. Ka-5 on the basis of that receipt.
In fact there is nothing to show that any demand notice was issued at all to Raghubir Singh or to Sri Ram Pandey.
The order of conviction is erroneous, but the facts there were materially different.

In the instant case, the two particular amounts were paid into the hands of the appellant not only as being due to the Government but the evidence shows that they were in fact due to the Government and the appellant would be guilty of breach of trust, if he misappropriated that amount.
holding: The order of conviction and sentence is confirmed.
